name: Rafael Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on an ordinary factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the shift on circular knitting machines that make workwear fabric. Yarn feeds through a ring of needles, and I set tension, change feeders and check the cloth for repeating holes. I have a two-year technical diploma and I am the person called when a machine starts dropping stitches at full speed. Solving that before a roll is ruined is the best part of my day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the job sit alongside home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Nora works part time at a grocer, and we have two children at school and a mortgage. I am one of the strongest setters at this plant, yet the wage is low for a senior operator and we have less than a month put aside. Only a few similar mills are nearby. I use AI every day to search fault logs and compare settings, then inspect the fabric myself. My father taught me that a good trade should support a family, so I notice when it does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the mill crew that AI is a useful search box, but it has not learned to feel a loose stitch on a running roll. I would keep using it for fault logs without treating it like a setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead work to continue, but our mortgage is too close to the end of each pay packet. Nora’s shop hours can change, and we have less than a month saved. A quiet AI year would still make me watch the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the knitting machines and write down which fault-log checks prevented scrap. I would use those figures to apply for a posted shift supervisor role if its wage covers the mortgage and its hours fit school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household money, not the machine. A loose stitch is easier to fix than a missing grocery shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supervisor job change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might pay enough to get ahead of the mortgage for once. I would still walk the floor, but I would be responsible for two shifts rather than one. I need the posted wage before I say yes to more responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the AI tool already catch dropped stitches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It finds a page in the manual faster than I can. The camera catches a pattern, then I check the yarn feeder and the cloth. A screen cannot tell me which operator has been fighting the same needle all morning.

say: I would **say** AI helps find knitting faults but operators must inspect the actual cloth.
A **supervisor** post should pay for the extra responsibility it carries.
think: My **technical** lead role looks safe in a plateau, yet our mortgage leaves little cash.
**Nora’s** variable grocer hours and less than a month saved keep me watchful.
do: **Keep** setting the knitting machines and logging scrap avoided.
**Apply** for a posted shift-supervisor role only if pay and school hours fit.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline bills even while confident on the machines.
S0.quote: A loose stitch is easier to fix than a missing grocery shift.
fieldNote: **Rafael’s** daily AI use supports manual searches, while his high technical skill still rests on physical fabric checks.
His **senior** responsibility pays poorly, and the household has under a month saved with variable shop hours.
He would **seek** a posted supervisor wage rather than assume his present title earns enough.

steps.text: Keep setting knitting machines and recording avoided fabric scrap
Apply for posted supervisor role only if wage covers mortgage and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the owner that software can plan yarn orders and shifts, but a later automatic feeder should be shown to the operators before it changes staffing. A family trade needs real apprenticeships, not just a screen demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn a new feeder quickly, but if one setter covers four machines instead of two, my hours could shrink. Nora’s grocery rota may be changed by AI booking too. I want the new technology to work, but I need both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise a new AI fault-classification tool on old rejected fabric only if the mill gives paid time and the quality lead checks my labels. I would ask for a paid supervised feeder-maintenance course and enroll if offered with my current wage and a posted maintenance opening. I would keep my present shift while the owner decides and check local postings if no course place appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible lost shifts. I still want to be the person who knows the new feeder before it is installed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why practise on rejected fabric?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong label on a live roll can send faulty cloth to a customer. Old rejected samples let me see when the tool makes the same mistake twice. I would not let a new classifier decide a shipment until a human checker signs it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another local mill worth applying to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real posted vacancy, a wage that covers our mortgage and a shift that gets one of us to school pickup. I would not leave a current wage just because a neighbouring mill bought shiny equipment. There are not many mills to choose from.

say: I would **ask** operators to see the feeder plan before shifts change.
**Paid** apprenticeships should come with a posted maintenance job and a real wage.
think: A **four-machine** roster might reduce my own setter hours.
**Nora’s** grocery rota could shift too, so both household wages matter.
do: **Practise** a new AI fault classifier on old fabric only with paid time and quality sign-off.
**Enroll** in paid supervised feeder training only if offered with current wage and posted role.
**Check** posted local mill jobs if no course, only with mortgage-covering pay and school pickup.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours, eager to learn equipment safely.
S1.quote: I would not let a new classifier decide a shipment until a human checker signs it off.
fieldNote: **Rafael** embraces a genuinely new AI classifier but limits practice to old rejects and human sign-off.
His **paid** course depends on an offered supervised place, current wage and posted maintenance opening.
The **no-course** mill search is separate and requires a posted vacancy, mortgage-covering pay and school pickup.

steps.text: Practise new AI classifier on old rejected fabric only with paid time and quality review
Enroll in paid supervised feeder course only if offered with current wage and posted role
Check posted local mill jobs if no course and pay covers mortgage and pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AGI can plan yarn orders by 2028, but capable robots that load and mend cloth arrive around 2031. I would ask the owner for a dated staffing notice before the hands-on machines go in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most setting hours to disappear when robots can rethread and inspect rolls around 2031. My knowledge might help install the first machines, but that is a short bridge. If Nora’s shop hours also fall, less than one month saved will not keep the mortgage paid, and I would be awake doing those sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Nora and I would stop the planned camping trip, list mortgage and shop-income dates, and ask the lender about hardship terms before any payment is late. I would take extra paid maintenance shifts if offered and put part of that new wage into emergency savings. If my mill hours fall, I would apply for posted local machine-maintenance work only with paid safe instruction, a guaranteed term and wages covering our bills and school travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing most of my wage. I can move fast. A short installation job will not feed the children through every winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a used automatic feeder for your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with our cash balance. I would test one at the mill on paid time before considering any tool purchase, and the safety guard must stay in place. A cheap machine can cost more than a good wage if someone gets hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help if both wages shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother could collect the children for a few weeks if he is free, and I would ask him first. Childcare would let us attend interviews, but it would not replace the mortgage money. I would check any public help rules before counting a payment.

say: I would **ask** for notice before capable knitting robots arrive around 2031.
**Yarn** ordering changes with 2028 AGI before robots rethread fabric.
think: I **expect** a major setter-hours cut around 2031.
**Nora’s** shop pay may also fall, leaving the mortgage exposed with almost no reserve.
do: **Cancel** camping trip and list mortgage and actual shop income dates.
**Ask** lender about hardship terms before missing a payment.
**Apply** for posted maintenance only with paid safety instruction, guaranteed term and wages covering bills and school travel.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and awake doing mortgage sums.
S2.quote: A short installation job will not feed the children through every winter.
fieldNote: **Rafael** places the core factory risk at the capable-robot date rather than the 2028 ordering change.
His **possible** installation bridge must have a guaranteed term, paid safety instruction and enough wages for bills and school travel.
The **family’s** tiny reserve makes sleepless concern plausible despite his quick practical response.

steps.text: Cancel planned camping trip and list mortgage and grocer pay dates
Ask mortgage lender about hardship terms before a late payment
Transfer part of extra paid maintenance shifts to emergency savings
Apply for posted maintenance with paid safety training guaranteed term and wages covering bills and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the mill that five years is time to put experienced setters into paid controls training before the robotic feeders arrive. AGI changes ordering by 2031; capable machines handle yarn around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 51 at the hands-on robot date. I could work on feeder controls longer than on the present line, but there will be fewer posts. My diploma taught machine drives, not the safe isolation of a full robot cell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enroll in a recognised mechatronics course next year only if the mill funds tuition, pays release time, keeps a safe supervised cell for practice and the timetable fits school pickup. After passing I would apply for its posted controls role only if pay and shift cover the mortgage. If the mill offers no course, I would search posted maintenance work at the few nearby plants on its own wage and shift terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the later roster, though five years gives me a chance to prove a new skill. A certificate without a wage would be a poor trade for night classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on the cell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Isolating power, testing a failed sensor and restarting the feeder under a qualified technician’s eye. I can diagnose the old machines, but the new safety circuit is another skill. I would not put my hands in while a robot can move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Nora manage the children while you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would compare her confirmed shop rota with the course nights before I enrolled. My brother could help with pickup if he agrees, but I would not assume he is free every week. The training has to work for the family as well as the mill.

say: I would **ask** the mill for funded paid controls training before 2034 robots.
**Experienced** setters should have a fair shot at the posted controls work.
think: At 51 I **may** lose a setter role despite my diploma.
A **controls** post needs a real wage and safe new instruction.
do: **Take** recognised controls course only with tuition funding, paid release, safe practice and pickup.
**Apply** after passing for posted controls work only if wage and shift cover mortgage.
**Seek** nearby posted maintenance work if no course, checking pay and school hours.
feel: **Anxious** about later shifts, able to test a funded route.
S3.quote: A certificate without a wage would be a poor trade for night classes.
fieldNote: **Rafael** distinguishes his existing drive knowledge from new robot-cell isolation and sensor work.
**Course** acceptance depends on funding, paid release, supervised safety and a confirmed family timetable.
The **maintenance** fallback has its own posted wage and school-hour tests if the mill offers no place.

steps.text: Take recognised controls course only with funding paid release safe practice and pickup
Apply for posted mill controls work after passing only if pay and shift cover mortgage
Check posted nearby maintenance work if no course and pay covers mortgage and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade is enough to build proper apprenticeships if owners post the wages and make room for working parents. I would ask the mill for a dated robot plan, not a poster about progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 at the 2036 thinking-AI date and 56 around the 2039 robot date. The children will be older, but the mortgage may not be gone. I want a real controls job by then and a cushion built from work, not a promise that somebody will look after us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present lead shift while taking a funded recognised controls course if paid release and supervised safety practice are offered and school hours fit. After qualifying I would apply for a posted local controls role only if the wage covers our bills and the shift works at home; if no course is offered, I would check posted operator work separately. From each newly paid overtime shift I would put a fixed amount toward our car loan after regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our wages even with ten years. There are too few nearby mills and too little cash to treat a future job as certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start your own workshop instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paid repair orders cover tools, rent and our mortgage after all costs. I like a risk I can measure, but I will not sign a lease while our savings are under a month. A workshop with no customers is a bill, not a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to test a real fabric roll, not just copy a screen. Ask what a qualified setter earns and whether the shift lets you live with your family. A trade ought to pay for the people who do it.

say: I would **ask** for posted apprenticeships and a dated robot staffing plan.
A **trade** should pay enough for skilled workers and their families.
think: At 53 in 2036 I **may** still lead a line while order software changes.
At 56 **near** 2039, I need a real controls wage if robots handle yarn.
do: **Complete** funded recognised controls training only with paid release, safety supervision and pickup.
**Apply** for posted bill-covering controls work, or separate bill-covering operator work if no course is offered.
**Pay** extra car-loan principal from newly paid overtime after regular bills.
feel: **Anxious** about long-run income with a thin reserve and few nearby mills.
S4.quote: A workshop with no customers is a bill, not a business.
fieldNote: **Rafael’s** risk appetite is bounded by actual repair customers and a household cash reserve under one month.
He would **learn** controls only with funded paid time, safe practice and school-compatible hours.
His **no-course** operator search is separate from controls applications; extra debt payment uses new overtime wages.

steps.text: Take funded recognised controls course only with paid release safe practice and pickup
Apply for posted local controls work after passing only if pay and shifts cover bills
Check posted operator work if no course and pay covers mortgage and school hours fit
Pay extra car-loan principal from newly earned overtime after bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most because capable robots could remove most knitting-setter hours around 2031 while Nora’s shop shifts may also shrink. Paid safe controls training and a posted mortgage-covering job would help us keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the cloth looks like after a screen calls a roll good. A machine can count stitches, but someone has to tell a family why the work still pays so little.

headlineQuote: A machine can count stitches, but someone has to tell a family why the work still pays so little.
portrait: **Rafael** Haddad, 43, leads a circular knitting shift and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He and **grocer** partner Nora have two school-age children, a mortgage, low senior-operator pay and under a month saved.
He **uses** AI daily for fault logs but inspects fabric himself and wants paid practical apprenticeships.
**Even** a plateau leaves him anxious about bills; capable robots around 2031 threaten the skilled setting role.
He **seeks** funded safe controls training and posted bill-covering work, with separate fallbacks if the course is unavailable.
biggestWorry: **Fast** AGI could remove most knitting-setter hours around 2031 while the family has under one month saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** safe controls training and a posted local role with mortgage-covering pay would help.
